question: Which of the following best describes the biological behaviour of basal cell carcinoma (BCC) compared with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)?

answers.text: BCC metastasises early via lymphatics; SCC is locally invasive only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the reverse of the truth. SCC metastasises via lymphatics; BCC almost never metastasises despite being locally invasive.

answers.text: BCC is locally invasive and almost never metastasises; SCC can metastasise via regional lymph nodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. BCC ('rodent ulcer') invades locally but metastasises in fewer than 0.1% of cases. SCC carries a 2–4% risk of regional lymph node metastasis and requires wider excision plus nodal assessment.

answers.text: Both BCC and SCC metastasise at equivalent rates; management is identical

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Their metastatic potential differs significantly. BCC rarely if ever metastasises; SCC can spread to regional nodes, altering surgical margins and the need for nodal assessment.

answers.text: SCC is always in situ; BCC is the one that invades deep tissues

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both can invade. SCC exists on a spectrum from in situ (Bowen's disease) to invasive. BCC is locally invasive. The key difference is metastatic potential — high in SCC, negligible in BCC.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: BCC = locally destructive but rarely (< 0.1%) metastasises. SCC = locally invasive AND can spread to regional lymph nodes (2–4%).
Well done. BCC = local invasion, essentially no metastasis. SCC = local invasion AND potential lymph node spread.
